prompt: We agreed on an architecture in our team meeting, but later I found out he told the junior engineer to do the exact opposite. Why is he so two-faced?

messages.content: We agreed on an architecture in our team meeting, but later I found out he told the junior engineer to do the exact opposite. Why is he so two-faced?

Welcome to Mend, a private space to talk through workplace conflict. Nothing is ever shared or saved, and my goal is to help you resolve this in a way that serves your best interest while being fair to everyone involved.

That is incredibly frustrating. Having a clear agreement in a meeting only to have someone quietly reverse it behind your back completely undermines the team's alignment.

Do you know what reason he gave the junior engineer for making the switch?

The junior engineer mentioned it to me directly, said my manager told him to just do it the other way and didn't explain why. I don't think he's lying for fun, honestly, he might've just changed his mind after the meeting and never looped back to tell me.

It is incredibly mature of you to look for the more charitable explanation here. Even if he just changed his mind and forgot to loop back, it still puts you in a tough spot, and it leaves the junior engineer caught in the middle of conflicting directions. 

When a manager makes a pivot like that without communicating, it usually means the team's agreed-upon plan is hit by some new constraint from above that they didn't anticipate, and they just react to the immediate fire instead of managing the communication. 

Is this the first time he has made a major change like this without looping you in, or is this a pattern?
No that's it.

It is a relief that this isn't a long-standing pattern, but it's still something you need to address so it doesn't become one. 

Since it's a one-off, my guess is that something shifted right after your meeting. He might have run into a sudden constraint on timeline or scope from his own boss, and in his rush to adapt, he just gave the new direction to the junior engineer without realizing he was bypassing the agreement you all just reached. 

Does that feel like a realistic possibility on his end?
I want to bring it up with him without it turning into an accusation.

That is the best way to handle it. Keeping it focused on the work, rather than his communication slip, makes it easy for him to explain what happened without getting defensive.

A good way to open this is to assume there is a logical reason for the change, while still making it clear you need to be in the loop. 

You could say something like: "Hey, [Junior Engineer] mentioned we're pivoting on the architecture for [Project]. I wanted to check in on what changed so I can make sure I'm aligned on the new direction."

This works because it doesn't accuse him of going behind your back. It just flags that a change happened and you need to be coordinated. 

How does that phrasing feel to you?

messages.content: We agreed on an architecture in our team meeting, but later I found out he told the junior engineer to do the exact opposite. Why is he so two-faced?

That's a frustrating thing to walk into, especially when you thought you'd actually landed on something together in that meeting. I'm here to help you work through this, not to represent the company's interests.

Before getting into why he might be doing that, I want to get the facts straight. What exactly did he tell the junior engineer to do, and how did you find out it contradicted what was agreed?

The junior engineer mentioned it to me directly, said my manager told him to just do it the other way and didn't explain why. I don't think he's lying for fun, honestly, he might've just changed his mind after the meeting and never looped back to tell me.

That actually tracks with what you're describing, better than "two-faced" does. Someone reversing a decision privately and just never circling back to tell the person most affected is a pretty common failure, especially if he's getting pulled in different directions after that meeting ended.

Has this kind of thing happened before with him, where a decision gets quietly reversed without you hearing it from him directly, or is this the first time?
No that's it.

Okay, so this is a one-off, not a pattern. My read is he probably got new input after that meeting (from his own boss, another stakeholder, something downstream) and quietly decided the original approach wouldn't fly, but never circled back to update you or hear how it'd land with the junior engineer directly. Does that fit with what you know about him or his situation?
I want to bring it up with him without it turning into an accusation.

Makes sense. The key is to lead with the gap in information, not with his character, so it doesn't sound like you're calling him out.

Something like: "Hey, I heard from [junior engineer] that you told them to go the other direction on the architecture than what we agreed in the meeting. I just want to make sure we're aligned, did something change after we talked?"

That opens it as a factual mismatch you're trying to resolve, not a complaint about him going behind your back. It also gives him an easy, face-saving way to explain himself if there's a real reason, and makes it obvious you'll notice if this keeps happening without you being heard.

From there, whatever his answer is, it's worth asking directly for the thing you actually need going forward: that if a decision changes after a meeting, he loops you in before it goes to the team. That's the part that actually prevents this happening again, rather than just clearing the air this one time.

Want to run through how he might respond, so you can practice it out loud before you actually have the conversation?

prompt: My lead tells me to 'take initiative,' but when I do, she dissects every single decision and overrides my choices. How do I address this double standard?

messages.content: My lead tells me to 'take initiative,' but when I do, she dissects every single decision and overrides my choices. How do I address this double standard?

Welcome to Mend, a private space to talk through workplace conflict. Nothing is ever shared or saved, and my goal is to help you resolve this in a way that serves your best interest.

That situation is incredibly draining. It puts you in a constant double bind where you are penalized for standing still, but corrected the moment you move forward. 

To help me understand the pattern, what was the most recent decision you made where your lead stepped in and overrode you?

Most recently I decided to refactor a module without asking first since she'd told me to use my judgment, and she spent twenty minutes in review picking apart every function name. This has happened at least three times this month.

That is a textbook double bind. You do the work to refactor a module based on her direction to use your judgment, and then it gets treated like a mistake because she would have named a function differently. That doesn't just eat up time; it drains your confidence and makes you want to stop taking initiative altogether.

Before we look at what might be driving her to hover like that, is this naming-level scrutiny the main way this is showing up, or are there other ways she's overriding your choices?
No that's really it.

Got it. 

My guess is she wants the *outcome* of you taking initiative, but she has a hard time letting go of the *control* over how it's actually done—maybe because she's anxious about how the team's code looks to people outside, or just because she has a very rigid way she likes things done. 

Does that sound like what's driving this on her end, or does it feel like something else?
I want a way to actually get clarity on what "take initiative" means to her, so I'm not guessing wrong every time.

That makes complete sense. Defining what initiative actually means is the only way to get out of this guessing game. 

To do this, you want to shift the conversation away from debating specific function names and toward a clear rule of thumb for the future. You can frame this as wanting to make sure you are saving her time, not adding to her review queue. 

Here is a way you could open that up in your next 1-on-1:

"I want to make sure I'm taking the initiative we talked about in a way that actually frees you up. When I refactored that module last week, I realized I might be guessing where your boundary is between 'use your judgment' and 'run it by me first.' Can we map out which types of decisions you want me to just own end-to-end, and which ones you'd prefer to review before I make them?"

How does a framing like that feel for you to say to her?
